An update on Microsoft's approach to Do Not Track

Okay, I've erased about 5 posts I've tried to make here. I can't come to a conclusion.

This isn't going to spare them bad PR for this action, if anything it's going to bring more attention to it. The people who are going to freak out about something like this are not the sort to be swayed by some post on the intricacies of a standard. Microsoft, so far as I can consider, is not going to meaningfully materially benefit from this. Their marketshare in browsers is small and growing smaller by the day. And while they may have a number of services and offerings that would benefit from tracking, it's likely to be at best a marginal benefit. Trying to make disabled tracking a standard would be a great way to attack some of their competitors that are more ad-driven than Microsoft.

I'm left to conclude this is actually somehow being done for reasons that are closer to the surface than my kneejerk reaction after reading it the first time.

It's a "do not track flag" which gets sent to the server, which requests they not track you, but can't actually prevent this tracking one way or another.

As you suggest, Microsoft could use this matter to attack their more ad-driven competitors and I think they did do so in this with one of IE10's selling points being "hey look - our browser has do-not-track enabled by default!"

However, as was said at the time, and as they seem to have now accepted, having it enabled by default means that it wasn't actually an explicit choice of the user, and so advertisers could've argued that they should just ignore the do-not-track flag being sent by IE (because they had no way of telling whether the user had made that choice or not).

Anyway - it's all moot in any case; I very much doubt anyone will respect the do-not-track flag.

If they really want to ensure the setting 'reflects a deliberate choice by the user', then there should be a modal dialog box forcing the user to make a choice before they can start browsing. From my understang of the article, it will default to track and only provide information on how to change it, the user will need to go into the browser settings themselves to change this.
Oh no, the advertisers will no longer have a DNT message to ignore!
